brand.title: IQVIA (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to Social Selling Techniques

questions.question: According to the Social Style framework, what are the two axes used to identify buyer styles?
choices: Personality and intelligence
Ask versus Tell and Task versus People
Speed and accuracy
Emotion and logic
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the X axis (Ask vs. Tell) and Y axis (Task vs. People) form the foundation of the entire model.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The framework is built on observable communication behavior, not personality labels or psychological traits. The two axes are Ask vs. Tell (how someone gets what they want) and Task vs. People (what drives their behavior).

questions.question: What is the signature question that a Driver typically asks?
choices: Why?
How?
What?
Who?
questions.feedback_correct: Drivers ask "What?"—focused on results, outcomes, and what they will gain.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style has a distinct signature question that reveals their priorities. Drivers are results-focused, so they lead with questions about outcomes and goals.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes an Analytical's communication style?
choices: Animated, tells stories, focused on vision
Soft-spoken, warm, focused on consensus
Gives direction, decides fast, focused on speed
Asks many questions, methodical, focused on data and accuracy
questions.feedback_correct: Analyticals are task-focused askers who prioritize accuracy, data, and preparation—they hate being caught unprepared.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Analyticals are defined by their Ask tendency and Task focus. They move methodically through information and care deeply about accuracy and evidence.

questions.question: What does it mean when a buyer exhibits a pressure behavior?
choices: They are ready to buy immediately
Something has broken down in the conversation and your approach needs to shift
They are not interested in your solution
They want to negotiate on price
questions.feedback_correct: A pressure behavior signals that something has gone off track—it is your cue to slow down, acknowledge what is happening, and adjust your approach.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Pressure behaviors (like a Driver taking over, an Analytical asking for more time, an Expressive getting argumentative, or an Amiable going quiet) indicate a mismatch or misunderstanding, not disinterest or readiness to close.

questions.question: Which of these is the pressure behavior of an Amiable?
choices: Takes control of the meeting
Asks for more time and more data
Becomes argumentative
Goes quiet and withdraws
questions.feedback_correct: When Amiables feel uncomfortable or pressured, they retreat into silence and withdrawal to avoid conflict.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style has a unique pressure behavior. Amiables, being relationship-focused and conflict-averse, respond to pressure by going quiet rather than by pushing back overtly.

questions.question: What is the primary reason to identify a buyer's Social Style early in a conversation?
choices: To determine if they are intelligent enough to understand your solution
To label them so you can ignore their individual needs
To adjust your communication approach before you pitch and reduce friction
To predict whether they will buy from you or a competitor
questions.feedback_correct: Identifying style early lets you adapt your tactics to match how that specific buyer prefers to communicate, making the conversation smoother and more effective.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The goal of reading style is not to pigeonhole someone but to remove friction by communicating in a way that resonates with them. Versatility—adjusting your approach—is the practical skill that drives results.

questions.question: According to the course, what is the relationship between a buyer's primary style and their adjacent style?
choices: The adjacent style replaces the primary style in certain situations
The adjacent style sits next to the primary on the grid and softens or modifies how the primary shows up
The adjacent style is less important and can be ignored
Every buyer has both a primary and adjacent style that carry equal weight
questions.feedback_correct: Adjacent styles sit in the neighboring quadrant and add nuance to the primary style—for example, a Driver with Expressive adjacent will be direct but warmer than a pure Driver.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The adjacent style is not a separate identity—it modifies or softens how the primary style expresses itself. Understanding the adjacent style helps explain mixed signals that might otherwise seem contradictory.

questions.question: Which of the following is the correct selling approach for an Expressive?
choices: Lead with data and detailed analysis, then ask to reconvene for evaluation
Focus discovery on their perspectives and ambitions, show enthusiasm, and minimize detail-heavy presentations
Respect their time, lead with conclusions, and offer clear options
Build rapport first, use we language, and never push for a fast decision
questions.feedback_correct: Expressives are energized by being heard, by vision, and by people—so make the conversation about them, show genuine enthusiasm, and keep the energy up rather than burying them in data.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style needs a different approach. Expressives are high-Tell, people-focused, and animated—so they respond best to curiosity, recognition, and broad conversation rather than detail or pressure.

questions.question: What is the key insight about versatility that the course emphasizes?
choices: Versatility means becoming a completely different person for each buyer style
Versatility is a personality trait some people naturally have and others do not
Versatility is a deliberate discipline of reading cues, naming the style, and adjusting your approach—not changing who you are
Versatility is only necessary when selling to styles similar to your own
questions.feedback_correct: Versatility is about deliberately adjusting how you communicate to reduce friction and help the buyer feel understood—it is a skill you build, not a fixed trait.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A common misconception is that versatility means being fake or changing your personality. In reality, it is a conscious, disciplined shift in how you communicate while staying true to yourself.

questions.question: How might a Driver rep's natural sales style negatively impact an Amiable buyer?
choices: The Driver's speed and directness will make the Amiable feel pushed and unsafe before rapport is built
The Driver's emotional expression will overwhelm the Amiable's reserved nature
The Driver's focus on questions will confuse the Amiable who prefers direction
The Driver's attention to detail will bore the Amiable who wants to move fast
questions.feedback_correct: A Driver's natural tendency to lead hard with conclusions and move fast can read as cold, transactional, and pushy to an Amiable who needs time and relationship-building first.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Style mismatch happens when a rep's defaults do not align with what the buyer needs to feel safe and understood. Drivers are direct and results-focused; Amiables need warmth and consensus—so the mismatch creates friction.
